summaries.summary: Knowledge graphs benefit artificial intelligence applications, consist of multi-relational triplets, and large-scale examples like WordNet and Freebase often suffer from incompleteness and sparseness.
Knowledge graph completion predicts relations from existing triplets, while a recent paradigm encodes entities and relations into low-dimensional vectors for algebraic reasoning.

Existing embedding methods struggle with sparse entities, and text-informed joint embeddings still face three problems involving combination, relation-specific text selection, and balancing structure with text.
The paper proposes a deep architecture combining structure and text representations with a gating mechanism and attention, outperforming baselines on link prediction and triplet classification.
The paper states that its contributions are summarized as follows.
This section briefly introduces background knowledge about knowledge graph embedding.
Knowledge graph embedding models entities and relations in a continuous low-dimensional vector space using a score function f(h,r,t) to distinguish golden triplets from negative triplets.
Existing methods differ between linear and nonlinear score functions in the low-dimensional vector space.
TransE is a simple effective approach that learns entity and relationship embeddings by treating relations as translations, with h + r approximately t when (h,r,t) holds.
TransE's score function is defined as follows.
Equation 5 defines f(h,r,t) as the negative squared L2 norm of h + r - t.
The embeddings h, t, and r lie in R^d, satisfy norm constraints on h and t, and are indexed by lookup tables.
Most existing knowledge bases provide entity text descriptions with valuable semantic information that can beneficially supplement entity representation.
Encoding entity text descriptions requires mapping variable-length sentences to fixed-length vectors using neural models such as NBOW, RNN, and CNN.
The paper uses three encoders, NBOW, LSTM and attentive LSTM, to model text descriptions.
The neural bag-of-words (NBOW) model generates text representation by summing its constituent word representations.
The text description is denoted as word sequence x_{1:n} = x_1,...,x_n, where x_i is the word at position i, and the NBOW encoder is given.
Equation 7 defines enc_1(x_{1:n}) as the sum of word embeddings x_i from i = 1 to n.
The word embedding x_i of x_i lies in R^d.
To address modelling issues with NBOW, the paper considers a bidirectional long short-term memory network (LSTM) for text descriptions.
LSTM was proposed to address learning long-term dependencies in RNN and maintains a separate memory cell updated and exposed only when deemed necessary.
Bidirectional LSTM consists of two LSTMs modeling text from left to right and right to left, with outputs z_i in each direction at time step i.
The combined BLSTM output at position i is z_i = forward z_i concatenated with backward z_i.
The LSTM encoder combines all BLSTM outputs z_i in R^d at different positions.
Equation 9 defines enc_2(x_{1:n}) as the sum of z_i from i = 1 to n.
The LSTM encoder has richer capacity than NBOW but produces the same text representation regardless of contexts, while descriptions and relations involve fractional aspects.
Because not all words or phrases are useful for a given relation, the paper introduces an attention mechanism to construct contextual text encodings according to different relations.
For each text position i, attention for a given relation r is defined as alpha_i(r).
Equation 12 defines e_i(r), alpha_i(r) via softmax, and the normalized exponential over n positions.
The relation embedding r, BLSTM output z_i, parameter matrices W_a and U_a, and parameter vector v_a have specified dimensions.
The attention alpha_i(r) is interpreted as the degree to which the network attends to partial representation z_i for given relation r.
The contextual encoding of a text description is formed by a weighted sum of z_i with attention.
Equation 13 defines enc_3(x_{1:n};r) as the sum from i = 1 to n of alpha_i(r) times z_i.
Since structure and text descriptions both provide valuable entity information, the paper wishes to integrate them into a joint representation.
The paper proposes a united model to learn a joint representation of structure and text information that can be trained end-to-end.
For entity e, e_s denotes its structure embedding, e_d denotes its text description encoding, and the main concern is combining e_s and e_d.
A gating mechanism decides how much the joint representation depends on structure or text.
The joint representation e is a linear interpolation between e_s and e_d.
Equation 14 defines e as g_e element-wise multiplied by e_s plus (1 - g_e) element-wise multiplied by e_d.
The gate g_e balances two information sources with elements in [0,1], and a gate close to 0 forces the joint representation to ignore structure information.
The model is trained with a contrastive max-margin criterion that favors training triplets over triplets with one element replaced by a random element.
There are n_t training triplets denoted (h_i, r_i, t_i), each with label y_i indicating positive (y_i = 1) or negative (y_i = 0).
Golden and negative triplet sets are defined, negative examples are generated by replacing h, t, or r, sampling follows Bernoulli distribution, and all parameters are Theta.
Equation 22 defines J(Theta) as a max-margin objective over golden and negative triplets plus eta times the squared L2 norm of Theta.
The margin gamma > 0 separates golden and negative triplets, f(h,r,t) is the score function, and standard L2 regularization is weighted by eta.
The experiments study empirical performance on two benchmark tasks: triplet classification and link prediction.
The paper uses WordNet and Freebase, specifically WN18 and FB15K, because their text descriptions are easily publicly available, with statistics in Table 1.
Link prediction completes a triplet with h or t missing and emphasizes ranking candidate entities rather than requiring one best answer.
Evaluation uses Mean Rank and Hits@p, with p=10 for entities and p=1 for relations, under “Raw” and “Filter” settings.
Hyperparameters include gamma in {1, 2}, d in {20, 50, 100}, eta in {0, 1E{-5}, 1E{-6}}, learning rates in {0.001, 0.01, 0.05}, and L_1 or {1, 2}0 distance.
Structure embeddings are initialized with TransE results, word embeddings by averaging linked entity embeddings, and remaining parameters uniformly in [-0.1, 0.1].
Final configurations are gamma = 2, d=20, eta =1E{-5}, lambda_s = 0.01, lambda_t = 0.1, and L_1 distance on WN18, with specified settings on FB15K.
Table 2 reports WN18 and FB15k results for “Jointly(CBOW)”, “Jointly(LSTM)” and “Jointly(A-LSTM)”, with TransE as the baseline.
The proposed models surpass TransE on all metrics, indicating that knowledge representation benefits greatly from text description.
On WN18, “Jointly(A-LSTM)” is slightly worse than “Jointly(LSTM)” probably due to limited relations, while on FB15K it achieves the best performance and significantly higher mean rank.
Although Hits@10 is worse than TransD, the models use a TransE-based score function and are compatible with other state-of-the-art knowledge embedding models.
Textual information largely alleviates sparsity and substantially improves Mean Rank over TransD, but may slightly degrade frequent entities and explain worse Hits@10.
For Hits@10 comparison, relationships are categorized by head and tail cardinalities into 1-to-1, 1-to-many, many-to-1, and many-to-many.
Table 3 shows FB15k results where models outperform TransE in all relation types, especially for “1-to-1” relations and predicting the 1 side for “1-to-N” and “N-to-1” relations.
To understand joint representation, gate activations are observed after sorting entities by frequency into 50 equal-size groups and averaging gate values in each group.
Figure 3 gives average gates in ten groups from high- to low-frequency, showing text information plays a more important role for low-frequency entities.
Triplet classification judges whether a given triplet $(h, r, t)$ is correct, with negative triplets constructed for WN18 and FB15K following BIBREF3.
For triplets classification, a relation-specific threshold $\delta _r$ maximizes valid set accuracies and classifies triplets by score.
Table 4 shows triplets classification results revealing that joint encoding models are effective and outperform the baseline method.
On WN18, “Jointly(A-LSTM)” performs best, while on FB15K its classification accuracy reaches 91.5%, the best and significantly higher than state-of-the-art methods.
Jointly learning embeddings of knowledge graph and text information has gained interest, with several methods using textual information for KG representation learning.
BIBREF3 represents an entity as the average of word embeddings in its entity name, sharing textual information in similar entity names.
BIBREF5 and BIBREF6 jointly embed knowledge and text but align embeddings on word level, losing phrase- or sentence-level semantic information.
BIBREF25, BIBREF7, and BIBREF26 use descriptions, names, CNN, or combined representations, with noted limitations involving word orders, ambiguity, separate objectives, and weight coefficients.
Works BIBREF27, BIBREF28, and BIBREF29 map textual relations and knowledge base relations to the same vector space with substantial improvements.
BIBREF30 proposes a similar attention model evaluated on link prediction and triplet classification, while this work encodes text description as a whole.
The paper proposes a united knowledge graph representation using structure and text description information, with experiments showing effective jointly representation learning with gating mechanism.
The authors state that future research directions will be considered to improve their model.
